hypotheses.title: Three-Check Contract Cut Set
hypotheses.claim: Appending exactly this instruction — 'Cap verification at three ordered commands: first run the narrowest check that crosses the changed module boundary with the greatest downstream fan-out, second exercise that boundary's nearest invalid or limit input, and third run the broadest affected-suite check only when its last observed runtime fits before a protected final 15% repair window.' — will improve held-out pass rate and regression count versus no appended instruction without increasing deadline misses.
hypotheses.rationale: The causal mechanism is propagation-weighted boundary coverage. A defect at a high-fan-out inter-module contract can corrupt many downstream behaviors, so checking that cut point before local details should yield more failure detection per command. One normal crossing check plus one boundary check samples both composition and exact semantics, while the three-command cap and repair window bound verification cost. The claim remains to be measured in paired held-out trials.
assumptions: Changed module dependencies and their relative fan-out can be identified cheaply
A normal and nearest-boundary case expose a useful share of contract defects
The agent has a reliable deadline signal and usable runtime history for the broad check
risks: Fan-out is an imperfect proxy for defect likelihood or user impact
A three-command cap may under-test large changes and over-test trivial ones
The nearest invalid or limit input may not represent the actual risky edge
Local implementation defects can be missed when attention is concentrated on one boundary
Absent runtime history can make the broad-suite admission rule unusable

hypotheses.title: Two-Pass Unsupported-Assumption Probe
hypotheses.claim: Appending exactly this instruction — 'After editing, inspect the diff once, name the changed cross-module assumption least supported by an existing test, predict one observable result that would falsify it, and run the cheapest targeted check capable of contradicting that prediction; after a pass, repeat for only the next-most-unsupported assumption, but after any failure spend the remaining verification time repairing and rerunning that same check.' — will improve complete task pass rate and regressions per tool call versus no appended instruction while remaining noninferior on deadline misses.
hypotheses.rationale: The causal mechanism is uncertainty-directed falsification. Rather than rerunning familiar checks that confirm well-supported behavior, the agent targets the two weakest inferential links introduced by its diff. Requiring a falsifiable prediction discourages ceremonial test execution, the two-pass cap bounds overhead, and switching immediately from a failure to repair prevents verification from discovering more defects than the deadline permits fixing. This is a testable proposal, not evidence of effectiveness.
assumptions: The agent can identify unsupported assumptions from the diff and available tests
Two targeted probes provide enough information to affect aggregate correctness
The cheapest contradicting check is available without creating substantial new infrastructure
Stopping after the first failure leaves adequate time for a repair
risks: Self-assessed uncertainty may be poorly calibrated and systematically miss subtle defects
The prediction step may consume time without changing which command is run
Two passes may be insufficient for broad multi-module changes
Rerunning only the failed targeted check can miss regressions introduced by the repair
The agent may choose an easy-to-pass probe rather than a genuinely falsifying one
